_comment: ORM result caching contract -- feature 25. One decision, OWNER-DECIDED
(OWNER-DECISIONS.md Batch 2, CACHE-DEC-01):
CACHE-DEC-01 (owner OVERRODE the drop-it recommendation): KEEP the explicit
Model.cached(sql, ttl) in Python/PHP/Ruby and FIX its invalidation, and ADD
the same explicit cached() to Node for parity. The correctness-critical part
is INVALIDATION: a cached read must never return rows a later write changed.
Three fixes, identical in all four frameworks:
1. BUST ON ALL WRITES. A save AND a delete AND a force_delete AND a restore
THROUGH THE ORM invalidate the cached read. Before this, only Python's
save() busted; delete/force_delete/restore never did; PHP and Ruby never
busted automatically at all; Node's cached() (which had drifted into
existence since the audit) was a per-class, untagged, never-busted store.
So a read-after-write through the ORM served stale/deleted rows until TTL.
2. TAG BY EVERY TABLE THE QUERY TOUCHES. A cached query is tagged with the
model's own table PLUS every table named in its FROM/JOIN clauses, so a
write to ANY of those tables busts it -- a multi-table JOIN cached on one
model is invalidated when the OTHER model writes through the ORM. Before
this the tag was the CLASS name, so a cross-model JOIN went stale. A write
to an UNRELATED table leaves the entry intact (tag-scoped, never a
wholesale flush).
3. ttl=0 (or negative) MEANS NO-CACHE, not infinite. cached(sql, ttl=0) runs
the query and returns rows but stores NOTHING, so every read hits the DB.
Before this ttl=0 stored a never-expiring entry (Python/Node) -- the worst
possible reading of 'zero'.
The explicit Model.cached() store is process-wide and SHARED across every model
(so a write on one model can bust a cross-table read cached on another). It is
the SAME tag-aware TTL query-cache subsystem each framework already had (Python
core/cache.py Cache, Ruby/Node/PHP QueryCache) -- ZERO new runtime dependency.
This is separate from, and unaffected by, the adapter-level auto-cache
(TINA4_DB_CACHE / TINA4_AUTO_CACHING), which stays OFF by default.
NO MOCKS. Every case drives a REAL database (a real SQLite file, real rows) and
REAL ORM writes. 'It cached' is proven positively: a DIRECT db write (raw SQL,
bypassing the ORM's bust) BETWEEN two cached() reads is NOT seen by the second
read -- the only way the second read can be stale is if it came from cache.
Mutation-proved (all four): disable the write-bust (drop the clear_cache/
clearCache call from save/delete/force_delete/restore) and every
'busts-on-orm-writes' case AND the cross-table case go RED -- a stale/deleted
row is served after the write. Make ttl=0 cache (store on the ttl<=0 path) and
'ttl zero does not cache' goes RED. Make the write-bust a wholesale flush (clear
everything instead of clear-by-table) and 'a write to an unrelated table leaves
the cached read intact' goes RED. Restoring each returns to green.
Each invariant names a REAL suite file per framework carrying the SAME case
names in each language's own idiom, which scripts/audit-contract-fixtures.py
normalises and matches.
feature: 25 - ORM result caching (fix cached() invalidation: bust on all writes, tag by table, ttl=0=no-cache; add cached() to Node)

invariants.rule: Model.cached(sql, params, ttl) with ttl > 0 caches the query's ORM instances in a process-wide TTL store: a second read within the TTL returns the cached rows without touching the database, PROVEN by a DIRECT (non-ORM) db write made BETWEEN the two reads being INVISIBLE to the second read. ttl <= 0 means NO-CACHE: cached(sql, ttl=0) runs the query and returns rows but stores nothing, so a direct db write between two ttl=0 reads IS seen by the second read (every read hits the DB). Identical in all four (Python Model.cached, PHP ORM::cached, Ruby Model.cached, Node BaseModel.cached).
invariants.why: The cache must actually cache (or the feature is pointless), and ttl=0 must not become an infinite-lived entry (the pre-fix Python/Node behaviour, the worst reading of zero). Proven with a REAL SQLite DB, real rows, and a REAL direct SQL mutation between reads -- no mocks: the ONLY way the second within-TTL read can return the pre-mutation value is that it came from the cache, and the ONLY way the second ttl=0 read can return the post-mutation value is that it hit the DB. Mutation-proved: make the ttl<=0 path store an entry and 'ttl zero does not cache' goes RED.
cases: a cached query is served from cache within ttl

invariants.rule: A write THROUGH THE ORM to a table a cached query touches BUSTS that cached read: after model.save(), model.delete(), model.force_delete() and model.restore(), the next Model.cached() of a query over that model's table reflects the write, never a stale/deleted row. All four writes bust in all four frameworks (before the fix only Python's save() busted; delete/force_delete/restore never did; PHP and Ruby never busted at all; Node's drifted-in cached() never busted).
invariants.why: This is the stale-read data footgun the feature exists to close: a cached read that returns rows a subsequent write changed or deleted. Proven with real ORM writes against a real SQLite DB (positive rows before, correct rows after) -- no mocks. Mutation-proved: drop the clear_cache/clearCache call from any of save/delete/force_delete/restore and that write's case goes RED (the pre-write cached rows are served after the write).
cases: a save through the orm busts the cached read
a delete through the orm busts the cached read
a force delete through the orm busts the cached read
a restore through the orm busts the cached read

invariants.rule: A cached query is tagged by EVERY table it touches (the model's own table plus every table named in its FROM/JOIN clauses), so a write through the ORM to ANY of those tables busts it: a cached JOIN over table A and table B, cached on model A, is invalidated when model B writes to table B. A write to an UNRELATED table (one the query does not touch) leaves the entry intact -- the bust is tag-scoped, never a wholesale flush.
invariants.why: The cross-model staleness (CACHE-CROSS-MODEL): before the fix the cache was tagged by the CALLING class, so a cached JOIN went stale when the OTHER table's model wrote. Tagging by table fixes it; the unrelated-table case proves the bust stays scoped (a wholesale flush would pass the cross-table case but is wrong). Proven with two REAL related tables (author/book), a real ORM write to the joined table, and a real ORM write to an unrelated table, all against real SQLite -- no mocks. Mutation-proved: tag only by the class (not the tables) and 'a write to a joined table busts the cross table cached read' goes RED; make the bust a wholesale clear() and 'a write to an unrelated table leaves the cached read intact' goes RED.
cases: a write to a joined table busts the cross table cached read
a write to an unrelated table leaves the cached read intact
